questions.q: Which chart is the default first choice for seeing the shape of a single numeric variable?
questions.explain: A histogram bins the values and shows their counts, revealing skew, peaks and gaps directly.

questions.q: In a standard box plot, what does the box itself span?
options: The mean plus or minus one standard deviation
From the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3), the middle half of the data
questions.explain: The box is the interquartile range, with the median marked inside it.

questions.q: The lesson's density plot of order values leaked below zero even though no order can be negative. What is the right takeaway?
options: Negative orders exist in the data
Smoothing does not know the limits of your data, so don't read the leaked tail as real
questions.explain: Kernel density estimates smooth across boundaries; the leak is an artifact of the method.

questions.q: A box plot flags 283 of 5,000 values as outliers in right-skewed order data. What should you do?
options: Investigate them; for skewed data the 1.5 x IQR rule often flags legitimate large values
Ignore the box plot entirely and never use it
questions.explain: The rule is a flag for a look, not a verdict; large values may be real and important.

questions.q: What happens if you draw a histogram of 5,000 skewed values with only 3 bins?
options: Nearly all values land in one bar and the shape is hidden
The chart becomes a box plot
questions.explain: In the lesson, 4,759 of 5,000 values fell in the tallest of 3 bars; bin width strongly changes what you see.
